title: Erdős Problem #1214: Prime Support of Integer Powers
description: Let x, y ≥ 1 be integers such that for all n ≥ 1, the set of primes dividing x^n − 1 equals the set of primes dividing y^n − 1. Must x = y? Answer: YES. Proved by Corrales-Rodrigáñez and Schoof (1997) using Zsygmondy's theorem on primitive prime divisors.

meta.author: Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof (1997), formalized in Lean 4
meta.assumptions: 4 axiom(s) and 0 sorry(s): order_characterization (multiplicative order ↔ prime divisibility), primeSupport_mono (monotonicity of prime support), zsygmondy (Zsygmondy's theorem on primitive prime divisors), corrales_rodriganez_schoof (the main result). See the Lean source for declarations.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem at the 1988 number theory conference in Banff. The condition 'P(x^n − 1) = P(y^n − 1) for all n ≥ 1' (where P(m) denotes the set of prime divisors of m) is called the **support problem**: two integers that look alike through all their power residues must be equal. The positive resolution by Corrales-Rodrigáñez and Schoof in 1997 [CoSc97] established this for the multiplicative group, and they simultaneously proved an elliptic analogue: two non-torsion points P, Q on an elliptic curve over ℚ with the same prime-reduction support for all multiples must satisfy P = ±Q. The support problem has deep connections to Galois representations, Kummer theory, and primitive prime divisors.
overview.problemStatement: Let $x, y \ge 1$ be integers. Say that $x$ and $y$ have the **same prime support** if for every $n \ge 1$, the set of primes dividing $x^n - 1$ equals the set of primes dividing $y^n - 1$: $$P(x^n - 1) = P(y^n - 1) \quad \text{for all } n \ge 1.$$ Must $x = y$? Erdős conjectured yes, and Corrales-Rodrigáñez and Schoof proved it in 1997.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof has two main cases. **Case x = 1**: then $x^n - 1 = 0$ for all $n \ge 1$, so $P(x^n - 1) = \emptyset$ for all $n$. The condition forces $P(y^n - 1) = \emptyset$ for all $n$, which forces $y = 1$. **Case x ≥ 2**: For most $n \ge 3$, Zsygmondy's theorem (1892) guarantees a **primitive prime divisor** $p_n$ of $x^n - 1$: a prime with multiplicative order $\text{ord}_{p_n}(x) = n$. Since $p_n \in P(x^n - 1) = P(y^n - 1)$, we have $p_n \mid y^n - 1$, so $\text{ord}_{p_n}(y) \mid n$. The key insight: $p_n$ does **not** divide $x^k - 1$ for $k < n$, so $p_n \notin P(y^k - 1)$ for $k < n$. This means $\text{ord}_{p_n}(y) \nmid k$ for all $k < n$, forcing $\text{ord}_{p_n}(y) = n$. As $n$ varies over primitively-covered exponents, one deduces that $y$ and $x$ have the same multiplicative order modulo every such $p_n$, forcing $y = x$ via a Galois-cohomological argument.
keyInsights: The **same prime support condition** P(x^n − 1) = P(y^n − 1) captures, mod every prime p, whether x and y are in the same coset of the group generated by x^n. This is a shadow of Galois-representation equality.

**Zsygmondy's theorem** (1892) is the engine: for x ≥ 2 and n ≥ 3 (exception: (x,n) = (2,6)), x^n − 1 has a primitive prime divisor p with ord_p(x) = n. This means 'most' primes dividing x^n − 1 'remember' the exponent n.

The **order characterization** p ∣ x^n − 1 ↔ ord_p(x) ∣ n is the bridge between prime divisibility and group theory. It converts the set-equality condition into a statement about multiplicative orders modulo primes.
The **elliptic analogue** proved in the same 1997 paper is deeper: it uses the Weil pairing and ℓ-adic representations to handle the non-multiplicative structure of elliptic curves.
The exception (2, 6) in Zsygmondy is tight: 2^6 − 1 = 63 = 3² · 7, and both 3 ∣ 2² − 1 and 7 ∣ 2³ − 1, so no prime has order 6 modulo it.

sections.title: Problem Identification and References
sections.summary: Module header documenting Erdős Problem #1214, its source at erdosproblems.com/1214, the 1997 solution by Corrales-Rodrigáñez and Schoof, proof strategy via Zsygmondy's theorem, and complete references [CoSc97] and [Zs92].
sections.mathContext: The 'support problem' for integer powers: two integers x, y ≥ 1 with P(x^n − 1) = P(y^n − 1) for all n ≥ 1 must be equal. The multiplicative group (ℤ/pℤ)× has order p − 1 for prime p, and the multiplicative order ord_p(x) = min{k ≥ 1 : x^k ≡ 1 (mod p)} is the key invariant.

sections.title: Mathlib Imports
sections.summary: Imports from Mathlib: Nat.Factors for prime factorization, Nat.Prime.Basic for prime predicates, GroupTheory.OrderOfElement for multiplicative order, ZMod.Basic for modular arithmetic, and Algebra.GroupPower.Basic for power lemmas.
sections.mathContext: Key Mathlib tools: Nat.primeFactors for the set of prime divisors; orderOf for the multiplicative order in a group; ZMod p for arithmetic modulo a prime p; orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one connecting divisibility and group structure.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines samePrimeSupport x y (same prime factor sets for all x^n − 1, y^n − 1) and IsPrimitivePrimeDivisor p x n (p divides x^n − 1 but not x^k − 1 for 1 ≤ k < n). Both definitions use natural number subtraction (x^n − 1 in ℕ).
sections.mathContext: In ℕ, subtraction is saturating: 0 − 1 = 0. For x ≥ 2 and n ≥ 1, x^n ≥ 2 so x^n − 1 ≥ 1 and Nat.primeFactors (x^n − 1) is the intended prime set. For x = 1, 1^n − 1 = 0 and Nat.primeFactors 0 = ∅. The definition handles both cases uniformly.

sections.title: Elementary Properties: Equivalence Relation
sections.summary: Proves that samePrimeSupport is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — an equivalence relation. Also proves the trivial forward direction: equal integers have the same prime support. All four proofs are one-liners using Lean's Eq.refl, Eq.symm, Eq.trans, and rewriting.
sections.mathContext: samePrimeSupport is defined as a pointwise equality of Finsets, so reflexivity (rfl), symmetry (.symm), and transitivity (.trans) follow immediately from Eq's properties. The direction x = y → samePrimeSupport x y is trivial (substitute).

sections.title: Specializations to Small Exponents
sections.summary: Specializes samePrimeSupport to n = 1, 2, 3, giving concrete divisibility constraints: primeFactors(x − 1) = primeFactors(y − 1), primeFactors(x² − 1) = primeFactors(y² − 1), primeFactors(x³ − 1) = primeFactors(y³ − 1). These are directly obtained from the definition.
sections.mathContext: At n = 1: primeFactors(x − 1) = primeFactors(y − 1) encodes that x − 1 and y − 1 have the same squarefree part. At n = 2: since x² − 1 = (x−1)(x+1), this constraints both x−1 and x+1 simultaneously. At n = 3: x³ − 1 = (x−1)(x² + x + 1), adding constraints on x² + x + 1.

sections.title: Order Characterization Axiom
sections.summary: Axiom order_characterization: for prime p, x with p ∤ x, n ≥ 1: p ∣ x^n − 1 ↔ orderOf (x : ZMod p) ∣ n. This is the fundamental bridge between prime divisibility and multiplicative order. The proof follows from ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd and orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one in Mathlib.
sections.mathContext: In the group (ZMod p)×, the element x has order d = ord_p(x) where x^d ≡ 1 (mod p) and d is minimal. By Lagrange, d ∣ p − 1. The iff p ∣ x^n − 1 ↔ d ∣ n is equivalent to: x^n = 1 in (ZMod p)× ↔ orderOf x ∣ n, which is orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one.

sections.title: Monotonicity of Prime Support Axiom
sections.summary: Axiom primeSupport_mono: for x ≥ 2, if n ∣ m then primeFactors(x^n − 1) ⊆ primeFactors(x^m − 1). The proof uses order_characterization: if ord_p(x) ∣ n and n ∣ m, then ord_p(x) ∣ m, so p ∣ x^m − 1.
sections.mathContext: If p ∈ primeFactors(x^n − 1), then ord_p(x) ∣ n (by order_characterization). If also n ∣ m, then ord_p(x) ∣ m by transitivity of divisibility, so (x : ZMod p)^m = 1, giving p ∈ primeFactors(x^m − 1). This is the key structural lemma for the main proof.

sections.title: Zsygmondy's Theorem Axiom
sections.summary: Axiom zsygmondy: for x ≥ 2 and n ≥ 3, except (x,n) = (2,6), there exists a prime p with IsPrimitivePrimeDivisor p x n. Also proves zsygmondy_exception_63: 2^6 − 1 = 3² · 7 (the single exception, verified by norm_num).
sections.mathContext: Zsygmondy's theorem (1892) uses the n-th cyclotomic polynomial Φ_n(x), which divides x^n − 1. For n ≥ 3 and (x,n) ≠ (2,6), every prime factor of Φ_n(x) is a primitive prime divisor of x^n − 1. The exceptions are n = 1 (trivially, x − 1 may have no new primes), n = 2 (x + 1 = 2^k is possible), and the single exceptional case (2, 6).

sections.title: Main Theorem: Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof (1997)
sections.summary: Axiom corrales_rodriganez_schoof and proved theorem erdos_1214. States: if x, y ≥ 1 with samePrimeSupport x y, then x = y. The theorem erdos_1214 directly applies the axiom to prove Erdős's original problem statement.
sections.mathContext: The main axiom captures the full Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof argument [CoSc97]. The key steps: (1) reduce to x ≥ 2 by handling x = 1 separately; (2) for n ≥ 3 away from exceptions, Zsygmondy gives p_n with ord_{p_n}(x) = n; (3) the same-prime-support condition propagates ord_{p_n}(y) = n for most n; (4) a Kummer-theory argument forces y = x.

sections.title: Further Context: Elliptic Analogue
sections.summary: Contextual note on the elliptic analogue from the same 1997 paper: two non-torsion points P, Q on an elliptic curve E/ℚ with the same prime-reduction support for all multiples satisfy P = ±Q. This requires the Weil pairing and ℓ-adic representations, beyond the algebraic tools used here.
sections.mathContext: For an elliptic curve E/ℚ, the 'support' of [n]P consists of the primes p of bad reduction or where [n]P reduces to the identity. The elliptic analogue replaces Zsygmondy's theorem with properties of division polynomials and Galois representations attached to E[ℓ^∞]. The Weil pairing provides the crucial non-degeneracy needed in place of the multiplicative group structure.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #1214 asks whether two integers with the same prime support for all powers must be equal. The answer is yes (Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof, 1997), proved using Zsygmondy's theorem on primitive prime divisors. The Lean formalization axiomatizes the four key mathematical facts (order characterization, monotonicity, Zsygmondy, and the main result) and proves trivially provable properties (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, specializations to small n).
conclusion.implications: The formalization provides clean Lean 4 definitions of the same-prime-support condition and primitive prime divisors. A future extension could attempt to prove order_characterization (follows from standard Mathlib lemmas about ZMod and orderOf), primeSupport_mono (follows from order_characterization), and possibly Zsygmondy (a significant formalization project). The elliptic analogue would require substantial new Lean infrastructure for elliptic curves.
openQuestions: Can order_characterization be proved within Mathlib's ZMod framework, using ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd and orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one?
Is Zsygmondy's theorem currently in Mathlib? It appears to be absent as of 2025; a Mathlib contribution formalizing it would be valuable.
Can the Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof proof strategy be completed with the axioms provided? The main remaining step is a Galois-cohomological or Kummer-theory argument.

crossReferences.description: Erdős #977 (Primitive prime divisors of 2^n − 1) uses Zsygmondy's theorem in the same way as #1214 — primitive prime divisors pin down the exponent n from the prime factorization structure of x^n − 1.

Quadratic reciprocity and the theory of primes in arithmetic progressions (Dirichlet) underlie the density arguments in the Corrales-Rodrigáñez & Schoof proof — specifically, that there are enough primitive prime divisors to distinguish x from y.
